summary: The Pag IBIG housing loan calculator turns the estimated value of property, the Monthly interest and more into loan-to-appraised value (LTV) ratio. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Pag IBIG housing loan calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pag IBIG housing loan calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports loan-to-appraised value (LTV) ratio in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (show other calculated values?); then you type in the estimated value of property, the Monthly interest, the monthly principal and interest and the monthly insurance premium.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pag IBIG housing loan calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Loan-to-appraised value (LTV) ratio=19 ÷ 20 − 1 ÷ 20 × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 1000) × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 2500000) × estimated value of property) ÷ estimated value of property)
Loanable amount=(1 ÷ 20) × estimated value of property × (19 − rounded up, ((1 ÷ 1000) × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 2500000) × estimated value of property) ÷ estimated value of property))
Loan amount=-1200 × (8916100448256000000000000000000000000 ^ repayment period) × monthly principal and interest × (fixed pricing period + 1200 ^ -12 × repayment period) ÷ fixed pricing period + 1200 × monthly principal and interest ÷ fixed pricing period
Estimated equity=((1 ÷ 20) × estimated value of property × (rounded up, ((1 ÷ 1000) × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 2500000) × estimated value of property) ÷ estimated value of property) + 1))
Annual Interest=(1 ÷ 100) × fixed pricing period × loan amount
Loan amount=1200 × Monthly interest ÷ fixed pricing period

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Estimated value of property = 10, Repayment period set to 30 years, Fixed pricing period set to 30 years (9.750%) and Multiplier for insurance = 0.0002. The calculator returns Estimated equity = 1, Loan-to-appraised value (LTV) ratio = 95 % and Loanable amount = 10.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Estimated equity = 1, Loan-to-appraised value (LTV) ratio = 95 % and Loanable amount = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Estimated value of property = 10 and Repayment period set to 30 years.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pag IBIG housing loan calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the estimated value of property, the Monthly interest and the monthly principal and interest — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pag IBIG housing loan calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns loan-to-appraised value (LTV) ratio, derived from the estimated value of property, the Monthly interest and the monthly principal and interest. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pag IBIG housing loan calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the estimated value of property, the Monthly interest, the monthly principal and interest and the monthly insurance premium, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter loan-to-appraised value (LTV) ratio in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Loan-to-appraised value (LTV) ratio opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Estimated equity = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pag IBIG housing loan calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
